mcqs.question: Which hook usage is the correct equivalent of `componentDidMount`?
options: `useEffect(fn, [])` — runs once after the first render
`useEffect(fn)` with no dependency array at all
`useEffect(fn, [someState])`
The initial value passed to `useState`
mcqs.explanation: An empty dependency array means the effect has no reactive dependencies, so it runs exactly once after the first render and never again — the same timing as `componentDidMount`. No array reruns on every render; a populated array reruns whenever that value changes, which is `componentDidUpdate`'s job.

mcqs.question: An effect's dependency array is missing a value that the effect's function body reads. What's the risk?
options: The component fails to compile
The effect can close over a stale value from an earlier render instead of the current one
The effect is guaranteed to run on every render regardless
React automatically infers the missing dependency at runtime
mcqs.explanation: The effect's closure captures whatever the missing value was at the render when the effect last ran, and keeps using that stale copy until the effect actually re-runs — this is exactly the frozen-counter bug covered later in the topic. Nothing about this is a compile error or an automatic fix.

mcqs.question: What happens if a `useEffect` that opens a subscription never returns a cleanup function?
options: The subscription is automatically cancelled whenever the component re-renders
React throws a compile-time error
Each re-run or unmount leaves the previous subscription active, leaking it
The effect stops running after its first invocation
mcqs.explanation: Without a returned cleanup function, nothing tears down the previous subscription before the effect re-runs or the component unmounts, so every re-run adds another active subscription instead of replacing the last one — a leak that compounds with every dependency change.

mcqs.question: Why can't hooks be called conditionally inside an `if` statement?
options: Conditional code isn't supported inside JSX
JavaScript itself throws a syntax error for hooks written inside conditionals
It would only affect that one hook's state, isolated from every other hook
React tracks hooks by call order, so skipping a call on some renders shifts every subsequent hook into the wrong slot
mcqs.explanation: Hooks are matched to their state by position in a per-component list, not by name — skip one call on a given render and every hook after it reads and writes the wrong slot, silently corrupting state rather than throwing. It's a mechanism problem, not a JSX or syntax restriction.

mcqs.question: In the `setInterval` counter example with an empty dependency array, why does `count` freeze at 1 instead of incrementing every second?
options: The closure inside the interval callback captured `count` as it was on the render when the effect ran (0), and never sees a fresh value
`setInterval` only fires once per component lifetime by default
State values can't be updated from inside a callback function
The empty dependency array prevents `count` from being read at all
mcqs.explanation: Because the effect only ran once (empty array), the closure it created captured `count` at that moment and never gets recreated with a newer value, so every tick computes `0 + 1` forever. `setInterval` fires repeatedly as expected — the bug is entirely in what value the closure sees, not the timer itself.

mcqs.question: An effect's dependency array includes an object built inline in the render body. Why does the effect re-run every render even when the object's fields look unchanged?
options: Objects cannot be used inside dependency arrays at all
The object is a new reference every render, and `useEffect` compares dependencies with `===`, not deep equality
`useEffect` always re-runs whenever any object appears anywhere in the component
The object needs to be converted to JSON before it can be compared
mcqs.explanation: An object or array literal built fresh in the render body is a new reference on every render, and reference equality is what the dependency comparison actually uses, so it reads as "changed" even with identical field values. Depending on the primitive fields directly, or memoizing the object, fixes it.
